title: 7.4 Self-Test Portfolio Review
summary: Reviewing one trade at a time is useful.
bodyHtml:
7.4 Self-Test Portfolio Review

Why This Matters

Reviewing one trade at a time is useful.

But after a week or month, you also need to zoom out.

A portfolio review asks:

  • What patterns kept repeating?
  • Which mistakes showed up more than once?
  • Were several trades actually the same idea in different markets?
  • Did my behavior change after wins or losses?

This lesson brings the earlier modules together into one review loop.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain the difference between a single-trade review and a portfolio review;
  • check for theme overlap, timing problems, and repeated behavior;
  • turn your review into one clear rule or adjustment for the next period.

What a Portfolio Review Looks For

Review area What you ask Why it matters
Results What happened over the full sample? Stops you from judging yourself by one trade
Theme overlap Were several trades really the same macro idea? Helps reveal hidden concentration
Timing Did losses cluster around certain times or events? Helps identify avoidable conditions
Execution Did position size, entries, and exits follow the plan? Shows whether process quality stayed stable
Behavior Did fear, boredom, or revenge trading appear repeatedly? Connects results to decision-making
Next rule What should be repeated, reduced, or removed next period? Turns review into action

(Table alt-text: A six-row table showing the main parts of a portfolio review and why each part matters.)

One Simple Example

Imagine your losing trades for the month include:

  • long EUR/USD;
  • long a Nasdaq or S&P 500 product;
  • long gold;
  • long Brent crude.

At first, that looks like four different trades in four different markets.

But if you learned Module 6 carefully, you should ask:

were these really separate ideas, or were they all leaning into the same softer-dollar, easier-policy, or growth-sensitive story?

If the answer is mostly one repeated theme, your portfolio review found something important:

  • the issue may be concentration, not just bad luck;
  • different symbols did not create true diversification by themselves;
  • your next rule might be to reduce size when trades share the same macro story.

That is the value of zooming out.

A Simple Review Sequence

  1. Gather the full trade sample for the week or month.
  2. Count wins, losses, and breakeven trades.
  3. Group the trades by theme, market, setup type, or session.
  4. Check whether losses cluster around one pattern.
  5. Read the behavior notes from your journal.
  6. Write one or two specific adjustments for the next period.

A good review does not end with:

I need to be better

It ends with something testable, such as:

  • No new trades within 15 minutes of a Tier 1 event
  • No more than two positions tied to the same macro theme
  • Cut size in half after three losses in a row

Why This Matters More Than One Big Winner

FINRA recommends evaluating performance over time, using a single spreadsheet if needed, and rebalancing as needed.

That logic matters here too.

One large winning trade can hide a messy month. One ugly losing trade can hide a solid process.

The portfolio review helps you judge:

  • the full sample;
  • the repeated pattern;
  • the actual habit.

That is more useful than staring at the single biggest winner or loser.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Reviewing Trades One by One Only

Single-trade notes matter, but repeated patterns matter more.

Mistake 2: Ignoring Hidden Overlap

Different symbols can still carry the same theme risk.

Mistake 3: Writing Vague Action Items

Trade better next month is not a review rule.

Mistake 4: Changing Everything at Once

A good review usually produces a small number of clear adjustments, not a full reset.
learningOutcomes: conduct a structured weekly or monthly review across themes, timing, execution, and behavior;
identify hidden overlap between positions or setups;
write a small number of clear, testable adjustments for the next review period.
